articles.title: MoCo DSA September Newsletter
articles.author: Metro DC DSA
articles.content: This is important. We’re all in this together. September 2026 Newsletter This is the monthly newsletter by the Montgomery County Branch of the Metro DC Chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (MoCo DSA). Interested in building a socialist future? Join DSA . Want up-to-the-minute updates? Follow us on Instagram , Bluesky , Twitter , and Facebook . Sign up for weekly updates (and see the archives ) from Metro DC DSA. Check out our linktree for important links, upcoming events, actions, and more! Take Action Fight landlord and developer efforts to raise the rent by sharing your story about Montgomery County rent stabilization . In 2023, the Montgomery County Council passed rent stabilization, thanks to organizing by Montgomery County DSA and coalition partners. Despite gains for tenants, landlords and developers are pushing the false narrative that rent stabilization has forced them to stop building. Use this form to share what stable, affordable rents mean for you . Upcoming Events Saturday, September 5 – MoCo DSA Coffee Social and Brunch. Enjoy a casual brunch at Emma’s Torch in Silver Spring. If you haven’t heard of Emma’s Torch, they are a non-profit social enterprise that provide refugees with in-depth culinary training as well as employability, equity, and empowerment training. RSVP here . Saturday, September 5 – Unite Here Local 25 Leaflet at the Montgomery County Conference Center. Join the MoCo section of the MDC-DSA Labor Working Group and Unite Local Here 25 to leaflet in support of a boycott of the country conference center until Marriott agrees to a fair process for worker unionization. This is a great entry-level labor action if you’ve been wanting to support labor organizing but aren’t sure how. UH25 staffers will be on hand to train and support you. Details here . Saturday, September 12 – Prince George’s County-DSA Labor Working Group Salting Job Fair. PG-DSA and the wider MDC-DSA Labor Working Group are hosting a Salting Job Fair. “Salting the workplace” is a union organizing tactic in which union organizers, known as “salts,” seek employment at a non-union company to organize the existing workforce. Interested in learning more? Get connected here . Thursday, September 17 – MoCo DSA Support Group. MoCo DSA would like to invite any comrades experiencing challenges and hardships to join us for an online group discussion focused on mutual support. Thursday, September 17 – Takoma Tenant Forum. The City of Takoma Park is holding its annual tenant forum. City staff will discuss tenant rights and responsibilities and share city housing resources. Montgomery County DSA and partners have been organizing to protect the city’s strong rent stabilization law. Join the meeting to show your support for rent stabilization and ask city staff questions you have as a tenant in the city. Saturday, September 19 – September MoCo DSA Branch Bike Ride Social. Don’t miss a community bike ride from Wheaton Regional Park to Lost Sock Roasters in Takoma Park. Not interested in biking? Meet at Lost Sock for brunch around 11:00 am. Saturday, September 26 – MoCo DSA General Body Meeting. Join online or in person at the Gaithersburg Library for our general body meeting to get updates on public-facing branch operations, working groups, and campaigns. Saturday, September 26 – MoCo DSA Happy Hour Social at Mayan Monkey Brewing Co. Join us for a social hangout immediately following our September general body meeting at Mayan Monkey Brewing Co. from 3:00 PM to 5:00 PM. Interested in building a socialist future? Join DSA The post MoCo DSA September Newsletter appeared first on .

articles.title: Who Killed Asylum?
articles.author: Levi Vonk
articles.content: Asylum as we know it is basically dead. The immigration system has been so systematically hollowed out that, for the vast majority of the world’s poor and displaced, it might as well not exist anymore. A brief list of what’s gone wrong: First, asylum approval rates have plummeted to historic lows, falling below 20 percent in 2025, compared to 55.5 percent in 2012. Second, the process is slower than ever before. A backlog of over three million cases frequently forces potential asylees to wait five or more years before finally appearing in court. In 2012, there were only about 300,000 cases on the docket, less than one-tenth of today’s, and wait times of just a year and a half . This backlog has led to a third problem. As asylum seekers are forced to twiddle their thumbs for half a decade, the Trump administration has invented increasingly elaborate ways to deny them a green card. In the meantime, asylum seekers cannot work legally or travel freely in the very country they are seeking protection in. This used to be a common and expedient part of the asylum process, but now asylum seekers must indefinitely put their lives on pause, something most cannot afford to do. Just weeks ago, in fact, the Trump administration moved to block asylum seekers’ right to reside inside the country while they pursue their cases, which, if implemented, could be asylum’s death knell. The once great universal value that every human being on the planet has a right to seek refuge would basically be no more in the United States. There are several reasons for asylum’s disappearance. One is the rise in xenophobic and racist rhetoric among elected leaders. Another is a lame-duck Congress that has been loath to halt the executive office’s attacks on citizens’ rights, let alone its attacks on the rights of poor foreigners who can’t vote or donate to campaigns. There is, however, a third, less obvious reason for the end of asylum in America: the fall of the Soviet Union. Refugees of Communism Only The modern concept of asylum was established in the aftermath of the Holocaust by what is known as the 1951 Refugee Convention. During the rise of the Third Reich, large numbers of Jewish émigrés fled Europe but were turned away by other countries, including the United States. Many later died in concentration camps. After World War II, asylum law was created to ensure that such a thing never happened again; anyone fleeing for their life would be guaranteed the right to seek protection in any other country on earth. Except that’s never how it worked. Instead, the asylum system was driven by Cold War geopolitics to push an anti-communist, pro-capitalist agenda. In fact, the USSR actually declined to sign the 1951 Refugee Convention, stating that it was simply another ideological tool “dictated by Western countries” to discredit socialist states. This was in essence correct. From 1951 to 1979, the US government overwhelmingly granted refugee status to people “from any Communist or Communist-dominated country or area.” This included some seven hundred thousand Cubans, four hundred thousand “Indochinese” (decamping after communist victories in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia), another four hundred thousand Eastern Bloc Europeans, eighty thousand Soviet dissidents, and almost no one else. It wasn’t until the passage of the Refugee Act of 1980 that the US asylum system became what we are now accustomed to, with migrants applying individually on a case-by-case basis. Crucially, this new asylum was available to anyone unable to return to their country of origin or the country where they last resided due to “persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” Still, throughout the 1980s, asylum approvals heavily favored applicants from communist countries while systematically rejecting those who were fleeing US-backed violence. Whereas refugees from Cuba and the USSR had 70 to 80 percent approval rates, Salvadorans and Guatemalans displaced by massacres and genocides funded by the Reagan administration had less than 3 percent. It’s worth noting that, under Ronald Reagan, the United States resettled more refugees than all other countries in the world combined. Even Reagan’s border enforcement policies look alien compared to contemporary anti-immigrant legislation, with the vast majority of the border left loosely guarded in the 1980s. It was common knowledge at the time that the United States relied on undocumented Mexican seasonal labor to harvest its crops and did not need a hard border to discipline labor’s movement. This likely informed Reagan’s decision to sign a bill that granted approximately 2.9 million migrants mass amnesty instead, the vast majority of them Central Americans and Mexicans. The decision had less to do with helping the victims of his disastrous Latin American policies than normalizing the labor market. While anyone who had entered the country before 1982 was allowed to remain in the country, farmworkers that had been employed for at least ninety days could also be legalized. Many of those amnestied were Salvadorans and Guatemalans who had already been denied asylum. As individuals, they were not worthy of asylum, but as an employable group, they were welcome to stay. The bill also put more money in border militarization initiatives and stricter employment guidelines. Far from an act of kindness, this was again a calculated political one. Having burned much of Central America to the ground in the name of fighting communism, Reagan had no choice but to accept some of the people he had displaced. At its core, then, the US asylum system has always been an ideological tool. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, and with it the gradual demise of the communist threat, the United States has been slowly dismantling it. Unlike the immigration system writ large, there is no serious material interest for capital in maintaining asylum. Without the threat of socialism’s Second World, the capitalists of the First World no longer had to buy off supporters in the Third. And now that capitalism has no overt global competitor, and the United States has abandoned any effort to legitimize its role in the world, it no longer needs to respect the human rights it previously claimed to be protecting on behalf of the so-called free world. Asylum’s Thirty-Year Decline The great unwinding of asylum did not happen immediately. In fact, asylum approval rates actually grew from 1991 to 2012. At the beginning of this period, the system was working at full capacity in order to put ideological pressure on a faltering USSR, whose migrants, fleeing the last gasps of the Soviet Bloc and the steep decline in living standards accompanying its transition to capitalism, were met with open arms. Indeed, rising rates of asylum seekers accompanied the growing instability of a freshly capitalist-dominated world. After 1991, there was a steady increase in globally displaced persons due to “persecution, conflict, violence, human rights violations or events seriously disturbing public order.” By 2013, there were over fifty million displaced people worldwide, many of whom were forced to flee due to proxy wars started by the United States. In 2025, that number had climbed to nearly 120 million, reflecting a level of worldwide conflict not seen since World War II. And that doesn’t even account for the millions of people displaced by climate change, driven largely by Western extraction and consumption. In response, there has been a bipartisan effort across five presidencies — those of Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden, and Donald Trump — to keep out the people displaced by failed neoliberal policy and US intervention abroad. Each did so not by eliminating asylum outright but by slowly eroding the rights that asylum is supposed to grant. One of the first blows to asylum came in 1996, under Clinton, when Congress passed the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA). Whereas migrants were previously guaranteed the right to ask for asylum at any time, they were now made to file for asylum within one year of arriving in the country. After that, their universal and enduring right to seek refuge from persecution would, paradoxically, expire. It was a wholly artificial barrier that served no purpose except to limit asylum protections. Clinton signed the law without hesitation. A decade later, in 2005, Congress passed the REAL ID Act. Under the auspices of preventing “terrorists from abusing the asylum laws of the United States,” the act demanded that asylum seekers provide concrete documentation of persecution in their home countries. The problem, of course, is that people fleeing for their lives across thousands of miles are often unable to maintain such documents. Nor do murderers normally warn their victims in writing that they are about to kill them. Though there was no evidence that terrorists had ever abused US asylum in the first place (none of the men involved in the 9/11 attacks were asylum seekers), the Bush-era policy set a precedent that asylum law was now a threat to national security. No longer needed to bludgeon communists, asylum was weakened to advance a new ideological war, and refugees became potential terrorists. But asylum really began to weaken under Barack Obama. After asylum rates hit all-time highs in 2012, Republicans ramped up pressure on Obama’s reelection campaign by falsely claiming that he had created “open border” policies flooding America with undocumented migrants. Rather than stand his ground, Obama capitulated almost immediately, deporting over 407,000 people in 2012 alone and 3.1 million across eight years, more than any other president in history, including Trump. Like Reagan before him, Obama specifically targeted Central Americans following failed US interventions in the region, most notably the Honduran coup supported by then–Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Under Obama, the court system was increasingly pressured to no longer recognize migrants fleeing gang violence as having a “ credible fear ” of losing their lives. As a result, gang violence, the main reason the vast majority of Central Americans sought refuge in the United States, no longer counted for asylum. Perhaps Obama’s most insidious innovation, however, was the creation of the Southern Border Program (SBP) in 2014, which paid Mexico to catch and deport migrants before they could ever reach the United States. The logic was brutal in its simplicity: After 1980, in order to apply for asylum, migrants needed to be physically present in the United States. So if they were intercepted in Mexico first, they’d never have a chance to ask. In its first decade, SBP quietly denied millions of migrants the chance to apply, without impacting official asylum statistics. Far from breaking from Obama, Trump continued down the path his predecessor paved. In 2018, Trump-nominated Attorney General Jeff Sessions ruled that gang violence no longer counted as “credible fear,” codifying what Obama had done out of sight. In 2019, the administration launched Remain in Mexico, which built on the logic of SBP by demanding that migrants had to first “apply to apply” for asylum, so to speak. Migrants would have to declare they wished to apply for asylum while still in Mexico, then wait there indefinitely until they were permitted to enter the United States and apply a second time. For most, waiting in a third country without access to work, social resources, or housing — especially in dangerous border cities — was an impossible demand. What Obama once did quietly, Trump did publicly and with relish. Relatedly, in 2019 the Department of Justice also passed what is known as the “third country bar.” In short, the bar allows the United States to pass the asylum buck onto Mexico by requiring that migrants who travel through a third country (that is, not their home country, and not the United States, but an intermediary between the two) apply for asylum there first. Geography dictates that this almost always means Mexico. Now US immigration judges can immediately deny an asylum claim if they feel that a migrant did not do enough to seek asylum there, even though Mexico is still actively catching and deporting migrants under SBP. This policy continues to implicitly favor those few migrants still fleeing communism — Chinese and Cuban migrants are much more likely to travel directly to the United States by sea and so have no third country requirement. Though liberals celebrated Biden for ending Remain in Mexico in 2022, less attention was paid to the fact that it was functionally replaced with a new phone application known as CBP One, which formalized and expanded the demand that migrants apply to apply for asylum. As soon as migrants entered Mexico, they were expected to download the CBP One application and take a geolocated photo of themselves daily in order to remain in the digital asylum line. Miss a day and they would be sent to the back of that line, which quickly grew to a wait of over six months. Migrants reported that the app frequently malfunctioned and crashed, losing their data and forcing them to start over after months of waiting in the third country. When Trump was reelected in 2024, he immediately closed CBP One without creating a replacement, leaving tens of thousands of migrants stranded indefinitely in Mexico. This was especially heinous because, due to an agreement with the Mexican government, migrants who enrolled in CBP One were granted a one-year visa in Mexico. When CBP One was suddenly cut, everyone was made illegal overnight. There are no available records of how many people have been deported from Mexico as a result. Weeks ago, the Supreme Court ruled to allow the United States to functionally eliminate all asylum protections for those fleeing US imperialism and intervention in Latin America. In Mullin v. Al Otro Lado , the court blessed the government’s use of a new “metering policy.” First invented and employed by the Obama and Biden administrations as another means of sidestepping asylum obligations, the policy permits an arbitrarily low number of migrants to enter the United States. Once that number is reached, the government can then refuse others to enter the country, and Trump can use images of those left behind to bolster his false claims of invasion. The transformation of the refugee program from granting benefits (including labor market access) to denying them has created a pressure cooker at the border, with tens of thousands of people concentrated in Mexican border towns. A key aspect of refugee resettlement was that it strategically distributed refugees to stabilize rural and postindustrial depopulation. Its dismantling was a disaster that set the stage for localized anti-immigrant backlash. The image of the refugee was transformed from a neighbor building a new life next door to a faceless mass clamoring at the border, providing grist for Trumpian immigration panic. Today only migrants from the last vestiges of communism stand a reasonable chance of receiving asylum in the United States. Venezuelans had a 72 percent approval rate in 2025, and Chinese applicants a 58 percent rate. Compare this to Indians’ 18 percent, despite Narendra Modi’s government, which is virulently anti-Muslim, being a key Trump ally. Asylum’s Last Gasp In 1990, as it became increasingly clear that there was serious instability within the Soviet Union, the US Congress created a new legal doctrine known as Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Unlike asylum, which is an individualized process that guarantees recipients protection for the rest of their lives, TPS, as its name suggests, was meant to provide temporary refuge — six to eighteen months at a time — for people fleeing particular dangers or disasters in their home countries. Once the country’s conditions are determined by the secretary of Homeland Security to have improved, however, the status is revoked and everyone gets sent back. This tool, like asylum before it, has been used as an ideological weapon to attack countries at odds with US foreign policy. For example, in 2021, the Department of Homeland Security granted Venezuelans TPS status, citing the corruption and repression of the Maduro administration. Importantly, US allies long known for human rights abuses — such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar — have never been designated as having sufficiently dangerous conditions. TPS was, in short, a way to sidestep the responsibilities and guarantees that come with asylum while retaining its ideological benefits. Now Trump has done away with even this. In August, the administration suddenly announced it was canceling TPS for Haiti, putting around 350,000 Haitians at risk of detention and deportation. The announcement followed the termination of TPS for twelve other countries, including El Salvador, Honduras, and Afghanistan. The Trump administration rescinded TPS for Venezuelans at the end of 2025, just months before kidnapping its president, Nicolás Maduro, in order to illegally seize control of the country’s oil reserves. Now that the United States is in control, and the communist threat has been vanquished, it is likely that asylum requests from Venezuelans, as with past allies, will plummet. This does not mean that Venezuelans and other migrants will stop trying to come. They will just have to come in a form useful to capital: as undocumented workers.

articles.title: The United Arab Emirates Is Devastating Sudan for Profit
articles.author: Husam Mahjoub
articles.content: At one time or another, Sudanese governments have hosted, armed, or tolerated rebels and opposition groups from all of the country’s neighbors, from Egypt and Libya to Uganda and Ethiopia. Sudan’s neighbors have repaid the favor, and a range of outside actors are now involved in the Sudanese civil war. Key supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) include Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and South Sudan. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea support the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the de facto government. Among all the external actors, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the most consequential, even though it has the least reason to be involved. Every other external actor has a stake in Sudan that derives from geography, security exposure, or the influx of Sudanese refugees. Even Saudi Arabia, while not a land neighbor, shares the Red Sea coastline with Sudan and has a direct interest in stabilizing its western maritime frontier. The UAE has no security interest, no shared border or river, and no reason to be concerned about refugees reaching Emirati territory. We can only understand its role in Sudan as part of a broader subimperial project that rests on four connected strategic pillars. Four Pillars The first pillar is economic hegemony. RSF-controlled mines in Darfur feed gold smuggled to Dubai, often routed through South Sudan, Egypt, Chad, or the Central African Republic. This gold can be monetized into hard currency that sustains the war while giving the UAE leverage over Sudan’s economic and political trajectory. Beyond gold, Sudan is also a critical node in the UAE’s continent-wide strategy of port and logistics dominance, part of an investment program now worth more than $110 billion across the continent, with dozens of port concessions, dry ports, and logistics hubs. Controlling Sudan’s ports, land, and mineral wealth is one of the reasons the war serves Abu Dhabi’s interests. The second pillar is political expansion. Sudan is a strategic frontier in the UAE’s broader effort to project political influence across Africa without incurring the costs of formal empire. A subimperial power is not a global imperial force; rather, it acts as an imperial actor within its own regional sphere while aligning its actions with the overarching interests of a global power like the United States. Sudan’s gold, its fertile agricultural land, its Red Sea coastline, and its sheer size make it a central testing ground for that project. The third pillar is the UAE’s desire to counter Islamist political movements and the influence of Iran. Abu Dhabi has been willing to cooperate with Islamist governments, including Omar al-Bashir’s regime in Sudan, whenever doing so served its interests, just as it has long functioned as a conduit for Iran to evade international sanctions. What its leaders actually oppose is not political Islam or Iran as such, but any political force, whether Islamist, secular, socialist, or democratic, that threatens their preferred regional order. The final pillar is a concern with regime survival and fear of democratic contagion. The roots of this concern go back to 2011, when the Arab uprisings confronted the UAE with an existential threat to its own model of governance. It responded by becoming an organized counterrevolutionary force across the region, intervening by different means in different countries. Such interventions included bankrolling the coup that brought Abdel Fattah El-Sisi to power in Egypt and backing the militia of Khalifa Haftar in Libya. In each case, a popular or revolutionary movement threatened a regional order Abu Dhabi wanted to preserve, and Abu Dhabi acted to reverse it. Sudan’s December 2018 revolution set off the same reflex. This was not because Sudan threatened the UAE materially, but rather because a successful democratic transition next door to the Gulf, achieved by ordinary people rather than by elites, might offer a dangerous model to its own population and to the wider region it is working to shape. Regional Network Most of the states that serve as the RSF’s enablers are not acting solely out of an independent interest in what happens to Sudan. They are acting, to varying degrees, on the UAE’s behalf, as part of a network that also extends to actors like Rwanda and the Somali semi-autonomous state, Puntland. Over more than a decade, the UAE has built deep financial and diplomatic relationships with the leaderships of these states. Those relationships are based on investment, infrastructure financing, security cooperation, and (in some documented cases) direct influence over individual government officials. The specifics vary from one country to the next. In Libya, the UAE draws on the territory, airspace, and military bases of Khalifa Haftar’s militia to move weapons and fighters into Sudan. In Ethiopia, Reuters has identified a secret UAE-financed camp near the Sudanese border built to train RSF fighters. Reporting has traced further UAE-linked supply routes for the RSF through Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, the Central African Republic, and beyond, as well as facilities established in Chad and South Sudan under humanitarian or medical cover that in practice support weapons transfers and the treatment of wounded RSF fighters. Other Players A few other external actors deserve a place in this picture, even if they carry less weight than the UAE. Qatar has historically supported the former Islamist regime and by extension the SAF, but there is no evidence it plays an active role today. Iran and Turkey have positioned themselves as suppliers and facilitators for the SAF, since there is no global arms embargo on Sudan’s national army. Ankara is concerned with trade, diplomatic influence, and defense industry outreach as well as agricultural concessions and port access. For its part, Tehran views the Red Sea corridor through the lens of its competition with Israel, the United States, and Saudi Arabia. Ties in Sudan that complicate things for those rivals carry strategic value. Israel has maintained discreet contacts with both Abdel Fattah al-Burhan of the SAF and Hemedti of the RSF as part of its goal of normalization with Arab states and its close alignment with the UAE. Russia began participating in Sudan’s gold economy through the Wagner Group militia, leaned toward the RSF early in the war, then reoriented toward the army to keep open a potential naval foothold on the Red Sea. Western Complicity None of the major Western countries is a bystander. The United States, Britain, France, and Canada have perfected the language of expressing concern while prioritizing their relationships with the Gulf states (and in this case, mainly with the UAE). These governments have long known, in detail, what the UAE was doing. Their own intelligence services and officials had access to the information they needed, and organizations like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch published detailed investigations. Media outlets such as The New York Times , The Wall Street Journal , and Le Monde have documented the UAE’s support for the RSF. The Yale Humanitarian Research Lab briefed the US and British governments and the United Nations Security Council repeatedly, warning that a siege of El Fasher by the RSF would trap over a million civilians and that time was running out. Officials in Washington and London knew the RSF was on the verge of capturing El Fasher and that mass atrocities would follow. The United States was hosting talks with representatives of the RSF and the Sudanese government at the very moment El Fasher fell, but it did nothing. France and Canada received reports that the RSF was using French- and Canadian-made weapons supplied to the UAE in Darfur, in direct violation of the UN arms embargo, and took no action. When sanctions did come, they landed on Colombians recruited to fight as mercenaries, but not on the Emirati companies and officials who financed and facilitated that recruitment in the first place. Imposing Costs Sudan’s own history of internationally sponsored peace processes offers a clear warning against the temptation to believe that the international community’s proper role is to engineer or force a settlement, whether through negotiations, power sharing, or externally designed transitional arrangements. That approach has been tried repeatedly, from the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) to the Doha Document for Peace in Darfur to the framework agreement that preceded this war. It has produced the same result each time: agreements that distribute power and positions among armed factions, promise development that rarely reaches the communities that need it, and leave the perpetrators of mass violence in place to fight again once the incentives shift. The role the international community is actually equipped to play is narrower, and more useful, than the one it keeps attempting to play. It can stop the states that are fueling the war through weapons, finance, and logistics. That would mean naming and imposing real costs on the governments enabling the RSF and first among them, by a significant margin, the UAE. The individuals, companies, and financial channels that move weapons and gold must be sanctioned, not merely the mercenaries recruited at the bottom of the chain. The assets of the UAE and of Emirati-linked companies are traceable and present in the banking systems and real estate markets of every major Western capital. They could be used as leverage instead of being deemed untouchable. The underlying pattern of regional interference has not changed since 2023. What has changed is that one actor with no direct stake and unmatched capability has been able to intervene at almost no cost. The actors who might have imposed a cost, whether we are talking about Saudi Arabia as a regional competitor for the UAE or Western governments with real leverage over it, have either woken up too late or chosen not to act at all. The Western governments in this picture cannot claim they lacked the information. They had the intelligence, the reporting, and the direct warnings, and they chose silence anyway. That is a decision, not a policy failure, made with full knowledge of its consequences. These governments, and the individuals within them who made and upheld that choice, should be held accountable, and investigated, as contributors to the crimes committed in this war.

articles.title: We Can’t Blame the Supreme Court for Congress’s Problems
articles.author: Harry Blain
articles.content: Almost everyone on the Left seems to have lost faith in the Supreme Court of the United States. This would have been improbable in 1954, after the Brown v. Board of Education decision, or in 1973, after Roe v. Wade , or even in 1992, after the court upheld the core holding of Roe in Planned Parenthood v. Casey . But after over twenty years of the conservative John Roberts serving as chief justice, including over half a decade of him leading a court with a 6–3 conservative supermajority, liberals and progressives no longer turn to the court with any real hope. If anything, they view it with hostility. Some on the Left — most recently Lisa Graves and Leah Litman — have portrayed the Roberts Court as a wrecking ball that has “rewritten the Constitution” and “dismantled our rights.” Others think that the court has never really protected our rights and that we were deluded to ever trust such an inherently reactionary institution. While these tendencies have overlapped at various junctures, the more radical critiques of the court have generally been confined to the socialist left: the pages of Jacobin , rather than the Harvard Law Review . Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan’s new book , Supremacy : How Rule by the Court Replaced Government by the People , is an exception to this rule. The authors are not only Harvard law professors but former clerks for two of the most celebrated progressive justices in the history of the Supreme Court: Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Sonia Sotomayor. Their book is not a tragic story of how the Roberts Court betrayed the great liberal traditions of Brown and Roe . It aims at something more fundamental: the almost unconscious and unanimous acceptance — by both conservatives and progressives — of the principle that the Supreme Court should be the final arbiter of all constitutional disputes. While Supremacy makes a concise and cogent case for an alternative vision of “democratic constitutionalism,” it misdiagnoses the problem we face. Its image of a Supreme Court constantly determined to aggrandize its own power is based on a selective reading of the historical record. As a result, the book encourages us to attack an institution that is not really responsible for our predicament. We are not cursed with a tyrannical judicial branch but a broken constitutional structure . The heart of this broken structure is the vesting of the preponderance of political power in a legislature that is designed to obstruct and delay rather than act. Our main task, constitutionally speaking, should be — and has been in the Left’s most successful moments — to push Congress to legislate on the most popular and pressing issues in American society. Attacks on the Supreme Court distract from this urgent priority. The Origins of a Strange Alliance The text of the Constitution is at best ambiguous about what “the judicial power” means. But as Bowie and Renan argue in Supremacy , the norm that seemed to emerge from early conflicts over the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction was that even if the court could and sometimes must hold state laws to be incompatible with federal law or the federal constitution (what the authors call “vertical review”), it had no authority to strike down acts of Congress (what they call “horizontal review”), which embody the will of the nation as a whole. This norm, the authors claim, represents the best balance between two vital democratic values: the empowerment of popular majorities and the defense of minority rights. Today, however, “our country is less a nation of laws enacted by the people than it is a nation governed by the decrees of the Supreme Court,” which has “seized for itself power over the most important decisions a nation could make.” Bowie and Renan call this predicament “judicial supremacy.” They recommend a radical rebalancing: the repudiation or limitation of “horizontal” judicial review of laws passed by Congress, leaving the Supreme Court only able to “vertically” review state laws. Bowie and Renan harbor no illusions about either the feasibility of this idea or the possible consequences of untethering Congress in this way. “It almost goes without saying that the Congress we have today is dysfunctional and unrepresentative,” they concede in the book’s concluding chapter. Their main objective is not to romanticize Congress but to demonstrate that “judicial supremacy has not achieved what its defenders say it has. In its scope and sweep, the Court’s actual practice undermines any claim that judicial supremacy is necessary to protect vulnerable minorities from acts of Congress.” If “judicial supremacy” has protected anyone, they argue throughout the book, it is the rich, the powerful, and the guardians of white supremacy. Bowie and Renan marshal plenty of evidence to make their case. Most of it comes from the Dred Scott decision in 1857, which ruled that formerly enslaved people could never be American citizens, until the end of Reconstruction. Frederick Douglass is a central figure throughout the book — and he ought to be, given his crucial intellectual evolution from the condemnation of the Constitution for its compromises with slavery to the belief in its remaking through popular interpretation. Supremacy also illuminates how Dred Scott initiated an enduring alliance between racial reactionaries and the Supreme Court, leading a Republican-controlled Congress to boldly assert its right to determine the terms of Reconstruction without judicial interference. Supremacy also discusses the early twentieth-century struggle between New Deal progressives and the Supreme Court, which culminated in Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s abortive 1937 court-packing scheme. Although Bowie and Renan sympathize with these progressives, they criticize many of them for attacking judicial review writ large rather than distinguishing between horizontal and vertical review. The failure to make this distinction, it is argued, made it difficult for some progressives to justify judicial nullification of state Jim Crow laws. This was evident in Brown v. Board of Education , when the strongly FDR-shaped court “proceeded as if the only question before it was whether the justices in 1954 believed that school segregation was constitutional.” This “conjured the image of a judicial angel hovering over and somehow apart from American politics.” Leftists, determined as they were to eliminate the scourge of segregation from the country, thus found that their traditional enemy — the group of nine unelected men in robes — had become their friend. If this strange alliance was damaged by Richard Nixon’s appointment of four justices to the court in just five and a half years, the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision gave progressives and liberals another motive for preserving judicial supremacy. As Bowie and Renan demonstrate, Democrats in Congress even abandoned a campaign to enshrine abortion rights in federal law because they were confident that the Supreme Court could do a good enough job after it (barely) kept Roe intact in 1992 — a perception that was reinforced by the confirmation of Ruth Bader Ginsburg to the court the same year. Arguably, at least some portion of the Left clung to the “guardian angel” image of the court forged during the Brown era until Roe was finally overturned in 2022. The Source of the Court’s Power Supremacy ’s encouragement of the broad left to decisively bury any lingering hopes about the Supreme Court is uncontroversial. However, the book reaches this conclusion by exaggerating the power and villainy of the court. In Bowie and Renan’s account, the court’s dominant historical tendency is to advance the interests of slaveholders, robber barons, and modern-day oligarchs by usurping power that belongs to Congress. But other scholars have effectively argued that the Supreme Court has had power thrust onto it, largely because the elected branches like it this way: they can pass controversial issues onto the judiciary and blame it for problems that are, at bottom, their fault. When Roe v. Wade was overturned, congressional Democrats didn’t apologize for failing to protect abortion access over the previous fifty years; they accused the Supreme Court of treachery. When Dred Scott infamously invalidated Congress’s effort to limit the spread of slavery through the Missouri Compromise, Republicans rightly assailed the court, but Dred Scott would never have occurred if Congress had actually confronted the slavery question in the first seven decades of the republic instead of constantly deferring and obfuscating it. Moreover, if we are going to criticize the court’s reasoning in Brown , we at least need to acknowledge that a Congress dominated by the Deep South had spent the first half of the twentieth century tolerating the Jim Crow regime while the court was mildly but meaningfully chipping away at it, particularly in the 1940s. There is a larger problem here. Congress was set up to fail by the framers of the Constitution. Even at the best of times, the equal division of legislative power between a House of Representatives elected on majoritarian principles and a Senate elected on minoritarian ones for six-year terms (and initially not elected at all) makes lawmaking a tough task. The British House of Commons recognized the obvious defects of such pure bicameralism by defenestrating the House of Lords in 1911. Likewise, the Australian Constitution draws much of its structure from the American model but gives the prime minister the power to force early “double dissolution” elections to both the House and the Senate if the Senate repeatedly obstructs legislation. This power was crucial to the passage of progressive legislation in 1974, including the seeds of Australia’s first universal health care scheme. No such mechanism existed to force anti-lynching bills through a reactionary US Senate in the 1920s; hence why civil rights activists tried their luck with the courts. Still, it was not inevitable that the Supreme Court would profit from Congress’s design flaws. Supremacy gives us a defensible theory for how it did — namely, by aligning with the forces of racial and economic reaction. But it might be that the court only did this in the late nineteenth century because those forces were dominant in US politics at that time. Then, as the forces of racial reaction in particular lost momentum in the 1940s, ’50s, and ’60s — buckling under the pressures of accelerating urbanization, the economic and ideological disruptions of World War II, and Communist and Third World condemnations of “racialism” — the court became more liberal. Many political scientists, going back to Robert Dahl in 1957, have observed the Supreme Court’s sensitivity to public opinion and to the politics of the elected branches. This sensitivity is essential to the court’s survival, because it relies on elected institutions to implement and enforce its decisions. As Alexander Hamilton famously put it in Federalist #78 , the judicial branch “has no influence over either the sword or the purse.” This makes it “the weakest of the three departments of power. . . . it can never attack with success either of the other two.” None of this literature is discussed in Supremacy , but the implication of the book is that Hamilton had it wrong. Many examples are offered of the Supreme Court attacking Congress, including the court’s nullification of the Missouri Compromise in 1857, the Civil Rights Act in 1883, the Keating-Owen Child Labor Act in 1918, the National Industrial Recovery Act in 1935, and section 4b of the Voting Rights Act in 2013. Such examples give the impression of a voracious institution determined to crush progressive legislation whenever it has the chance. The reader gets no sense of the fact that, throughout its history, the Supreme Court has generally been reluctant to invalidate federal laws, striking down 172 as unconstitutional in whole or in part since 1789. It has struck down state and local laws at least five times as frequently. Even the Roberts Court has upheld federal legislation when conservative ideology could have dictated a different result, including the 1968 Gun Control Act , the “ individual mandate ” of the Affordable Care Act, and the Indian Child Welfare Act . The court declared back in 1819 that its default posture in cases of horizontal review would be to defer to Congress. Most of the time, it has stuck to this position. Addressing the Real Problem Although this doesn’t mean that the Supreme Court is harmless, it does call into question the urgency and value of an attack on horizontal review. Such an attack would only be necessary if the court were consistently obstructing progressive federal legislation. Supremacy does not prove that the Roberts Court is doing this. It contains no dedicated chapter on the Roberts Court and no sustained analysis of its decisions. What kind of threat does the Roberts Court pose? To be sure, in line with Supremacy ’s thesis, it has exercised horizontal review in potentially destructive ways, notably in the areas of voting rights and campaign finance . However, this court’s primary target seems to be the administrative state rather than Congress. Moreover, it has demonstrated how vertical review can seriously hurt the Left — a danger that is not raised at all in Supremacy . Notable examples include the court’s decisions preventing states from mandating “agency fees” to unions in public sector workplaces, declaring state laws granting union organizers access to rural workplaces “ takings ” of private property, and invalidating state gun control laws . Curbing the court’s authority to review acts of Congress won’t help with any of this. The sad reality is that even if the Roberts Court wanted to go on a rampage against progressive federal legislation, it would have trouble finding any. For all his faults, John Roberts is not the reason why we don’t have federally guaranteed universal health care (including reproductive health care), paid parental leave, holiday pay, or a living wage. The basic theory of Supremacy would have us attack the Supreme Court for things it hasn’t done yet and may never do, all while Congress, the branch of government endowed with the greatest constitutional authority, continues its impressively consistent record of either avoiding or exacerbating our nation’s most pressing problems. On rare occasions, however, Congress has served the Left in the past, but only under intense external pressure. Beyond the obviously critical force of the labor movement, two institutional mechanisms have helped build pressure on Congress: the presidency and the states. The presidency’s potential role — activated most notably by the Left when FDR occupied the White House — is fairly direct: the president, though lacking in constitutional powers, heads one of the political parties in Congress, possesses a unique ability to act quickly, and can mobilize public opinion rhetorically. The states’ potential role (articulated in Heather Gerken’s theory of progressive federalism ) is more indirect, involving experimentation with progressive policies that begins in one state, spreads to others, and eventually becomes so widespread that Congress follows. Although a conservative Supreme Court might try to thwart such experimentation, it is both a virtue and a vice of our constitutional system that states can find many creative ways to escape the reach of unfriendly federal courts. They only really relent when Congress takes their federal funding away. One virtue of having such powerful subnational political units was evident in the early twentieth century, when states such as New York (not to mention many cities) pioneered the economic and social policies that would later become central to the federal New Deal. Perhaps it is uncomfortable for leftists to talk about activating the presidency while Donald Trump sits in the Oval Office, or to talk about using state power given the often reactionary history of federalism in this country. But uncomfortable conversations about these tools would be much more productive than our seemingly endless lamentations about the Supreme Court. Books like Supremacy , while admirably readable, are ultimately guiding us nowhere particularly useful.

articles.title: In Italy’s Financial Capital, Socialism Is Back in the Air
articles.author: Jacopo Custodi
articles.content: One in twelve people living in Milan is a millionaire. A report by the consultancy Henley & Partners ranks Italy’s second-largest city and financial capital as the world leader for millionaires per resident, well ahead of New York City, where the figure is one in twenty-two. A growing number come from abroad, drawn not just by the vibrancy of Italy’s fashion hub but also generous tax breaks for wealthy newcomers. For everyone else, Milan tells a very different story. The cost of living is soaring, and with rents and house prices spiraling out of control, working people are being pushed to the suburbs. Add to that the fact that the public health system is in crisis, with private health care giants opening clinics across the city. All of this has unfolded under center-left administrations that have governed Milan without interruption since 2011. These trends predate that year, of course. But in the last fifteen years the city’s center left has not merely witnessed the transformation but helped it to thrive. In spring 2027, Milan will elect a successor to Giuseppe Sala, the current mayor, who is barred from running for a third term. The right-wing coalition that leads the national government is staking everything on the claim that the city has become dangerously unsafe — even though police figures show violent crime falling . These parties still haven’t agreed on who should carry that message: Matteo Salvini’s Lega and Forza Italia, founded by the late Milanese tycoon Silvio Berlusconi, have each put forward their own name, leaving the final call to the coalition’s leaders in Rome. The center left hasn’t picked its candidate either. Everything points to a primary, likely early next year. This is where things get interesting. The contest hasn’t even been confirmed yet, but one insurgent contender has been campaigning for months already. Milan’s Revolution His name is Lorenzo Pacini. Thirty years old and a law graduate, Pacini serves on the local executive of the district covering Milan’s historic center. He belongs to the Partito Democratico (PD), the largest party in Italy’s center-left coalition, but his politics lie well to the left of the PD mainstream. His campaign is called “La Rivoluzione di Milano” (Milan’s Revolution). Its logo reworks the biscione , the serpent devouring a child that has been a symbol of the city since the Middle Ages, when the ruling Visconti family adopted it as its emblem. Centuries later, Berlusconi borrowed it for his business empire. In Pacini’s version, however, the serpent is swallowing a portly billionaire in a top hat. The goal of his campaign? What he calls “municipal socialism.” Pacini’s language is plain, direct, and concrete, far from the highbrow register that has come to mark parts of the contemporary Left, in Italy as elsewhere. Yet it is densely political. He talks about “socialism,” “the working class,” and “class struggle” — all terms that Italy’s mainstream left largely abandoned decades ago, and he uses them everywhere: in Milan’s streets, on social media, and on right-leaning TV and radio talk shows, sparring with hosts and other guests. He has more than a hundred thousand followers on Instagram, and several of his videos praising workers or talking about work have passed a million views. He also found himself at the center of a national controversy after appearing on a popular right-wing radio show, La Zanzara , where, in a heated exchange, he said that, if need be, fascists should be fought “with rifles,” as the partisans once did. His point was that branding the entire Right as fascist makes no sense, and that the Italian Republic was officially founded on the armed antifascist resistance. But the governing right, apparently recognizing itself in the label, kicked up a storm. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni weighed in personally, and PD leaders duly distanced the party from his words. This past summer, as a prolonged heat wave hit Italy and much of Europe, Pacini took his campaign into the neighborhoods with what he calls anguriate , meaning watermelon parties. These are open-air gatherings where he presents his ideas, listens to residents’ complaints, collects proposals, and hands out slices of fresh watermelon. The gatherings were initially modest in size, but they grew over the summer, and the themes he keeps returning to — housing costs, public services, taxing the rich — have begun to filter into the city’s political debate. He has also launched MiDecido , an online platform where Milanese can submit and vote on policy proposals: a way, in the campaign’s words, to “build municipal socialism together.” Pacini describes his family background as rich in cultural capital but short on money and says he worked his way through university as a dishwasher and a fruit seller, among other jobs. Asked who inspires him, he often names three figures. The first is Emilio Caldara, Milan’s first Socialist (PSI) mayor, elected in 1914, who, as Pacini told Vanity Fair , “taxed the rich and built the public services we still enjoy today,” including the city’s public transport company. The second is his grandmother, a member of the Partito Comunista Italiano (PCI) who taught in the party’s evening schools for workers. The third is Ho Chi Minh, whom he described as “a great revolutionary, a great patriot, a man who managed to free his country first from the French and then from the Americans, with an enviable political and strategic skill that should serve as an example.” There is a Milanese thread to this unusual last choice: the Vietnamese leader appears to have lived in the city in the 1930s, incognito under Benito Mussolini’s regime, working as a cook — a chapter of his life about which little is known. All this sits awkwardly with the PD. Even under the new secretary Elly Schlein, who has pulled it somewhat to the left, it remains a party of Italy’s liberal, moderate establishment, and all the more so in Milan, where it governs, and where the national leadership’s modest leftward shift has made little concrete difference. Pacini, however, doesn’t believe he’s the one who should feel out of place. “It’s those who still push essentially centrist ideas,” he told major Italian weekly L’Espresso , who shouldn’t feel at home in a left party.” An Uphill Primary Winning the center-left coalition primary won’t be easy. The favorite of the city’s establishment is Mario Calabresi, a centrist and a leading figure in Italy’s media world, former editor of two of the country’s biggest newspapers, La Stampa and then La Repubblica , who is backed by a sizeable part of the PD itself. On his own flank, Pacini will likely face Pierfrancesco Majorino, the PD’s group leader in the Lombardy regional council and a close ally of party leader Schlein. Other candidates from the coalition’s left have also declared or are weighing a run, further crowding his side of the field. In a hypothetical primary poll conducted in early August, Pacini stood at just 7 percent . For a candidate with no party machine behind him and a campaign run by young volunteers, that is not nothing, but it makes him a long shot. Still, it is worth recalling that Zohran Mamdani was at 1 percent in the first poll for New York’s Democratic primary in February 2025, and that well into the campaign most observers doubted he would get far. Given his talk of “municipal socialism,” the Italian press has often compared Pacini to Mamdani. The candidate himself, however, does not encourage the comparison, and has played it down whenever interviewers have raised it. He grants that Mamdani’s story has plenty to teach but insists that every city has its own particularities and that copy-pasting models from abroad rarely works. When I spoke with him and brought up the case of Molfetta, the southern town that recently elected a communist mayor, he joked: “I think there are more people from Molfetta in Milan than New Yorkers — so maybe we should listen to them a bit more.” It was a nod to the generations of southern Italians who built Milan’s working class. He has a point, in any case. When it comes to municipal socialism, Italy hardly needs to import models. Before fascism, the Socialists governed Milan, Bologna, and hundreds of smaller towns, and the phrase itself was already current in Italian politics: it was the socialists’ name for what they were doing. After 1945, the Communists ran cities across Italy — Bologna above all, for half a century — building a distinctive local socialism of cooperatives, public nurseries, urban planning, and welfare that was, for decades, one of the party’s most persuasive arguments for its fitness to govern. Pacini, in other words, is reaching back into a tradition that his own party, now far from its roots in the workers’ movement, spent the last thirty years trying to forget. Whether Milan’s voters are ready to embrace it again, after decades in which that tradition was dismissed and demonized, remains to be seen. But deteriorating material conditions are sharpening the appetite for change. In a survey published this month, 95 percent of Milanese said the way the city is run needs to change, and 54 percent said the change should be “radical.” Pacini wants to prove that left-wing politics is not the pastime of a radical-chic cultural elite, as the Italian right loves to caricature it. If he can convince Milan’s population that municipal socialism is a concrete answer to their problems, rooted in the best of Italy’s own history, he may stand a chance.
